planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in a mixed border or foundation planting; this compact, self-fertile selection needs no pollinator and stays tidy without pruning.

directions: Iroquois Beauty (trade name for the cultivar 'Morton') was selected at The Morton Arboretum for its dense, rounded, low-suckering habit that stays far more compact than the wild species, making it a good substitute for burning bush in small gardens. White spring flower clusters give way to glossy black berries in late summer, and the dark green summer foliage turns brilliant red-orange in fall. It tolerates both wet and dry soils and is largely untroubled by pests or disease once established, needing only an occasional thinning cut at the base to remove old canes.

planting.note: Plant in spring as a low hedge, mass groundcover, or edging shrub; space plants closer together for a solid weed-suppressing mat within two seasons.

directions: Low Scape Mound is a dwarf, mounding sport of black chokeberry bred for use as a tough, low-maintenance groundcover rather than for berry production, though it still bears the species' white spring flowers, small black fruit, and fiery red fall color on a dense, spreading form under two feet tall. It handles wet, dry, salty, or clay soils and urban pollution better than most low shrubs, making it useful for parking-lot islands, slopes, and mass plantings where mowing is impractical. Trim lightly after flowering only if a tighter shape is wanted; otherwise it requires no routine pruning.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring in rows if growing for juice production; Aron is self-fertile and crops heavily without a second cultivar nearby.

directions: Aron is a Danish-origin black chokeberry selection that became the dominant cultivar in Eastern European commercial aronia orchards, prized for its upright vigor, heavy and consistent fruit set, and berries that hold well on the bush for mechanical or hand harvest. It grows taller and more upright than compact cultivars like Nero, tolerates poor and periodically wet soils, and produces little suckering compared to the wild species. Its high-anthocyanin berries are typically processed into juice, syrup, or dried snacks rather than eaten fresh due to their astringency; harvest in late summer once berries turn from red to glossy black.

planting.note: Plant in full sun for the deepest foliage color, in moist but well-drained soil; cut back hard in late winter to encourage vigorous colored new growth.

directions: Guincho Purple, originally found near Guincho, Portugal and holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit, opens with near-black spring foliage that softens to a deep purple-green through summer, setting off pink-tinged flower heads followed by shiny black berries and rich purple-red fall color. It is grown chiefly as an ornamental foliage and flowering shrub rather than for fruit production, and responds well to an annual hard prune to keep a compact, richly colored shrub instead of a lanky tree form. Site it where afternoon light can shine through the dark leaves for best effect, and give it the same moist, fertile soil favored by wild elderberry.

planting.note: Plant in partial shade to protect the delicate variegated leaves from scorch; this slow-growing heirloom cultivar needs less frequent hard pruning than green-leaved elderberries.

directions: Pulverulenta is a Victorian-era heirloom elderberry grown purely for its striking foliage, which appears dusted or marbled with fine white speckling across each leaflet, giving the whole shrub a frosted, variegated look distinct from any other elder in cultivation. It is noticeably slower-growing and less vigorous than green- or purple-leaved elderberry cultivars, so it rarely needs the aggressive annual cutback other ornamental elders require, and it still produces the flat white flower clusters and small black berries typical of the species. Give it some afternoon shade and steady moisture, since the pale leaf tissue is more prone to sunburn and drought stress than fully green foliage.

planting.note: Plant one male Pollmix for every six to eight female sea buckthorn shrubs, within about 50 to 100 feet, in full sun on well-drained soil.

directions: Pollmix is a German-bred male sea buckthorn selection grown specifically to supply pollen for female fruiting cultivars such as Leikora and Titan, since Hippophae rhamnoides is dioecious and female plants set little or no fruit without a nearby male. It bears no berries itself but produces abundant, early-shedding catkins and grows as vigorously as the fruiting cultivars, with the same silvery narrow foliage, thorny branching, and nitrogen-fixing roots that let it thrive in poor, sandy, or coastal soils. One Pollmix plant can pollinate a substantial block of female shrubs, so it is typically planted upwind of the orchard or hedge to aid pollen dispersal.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic soil such as a pond edge, bog garden, or low woodland area; amend with peat or pine bark if native soil is not already acidic.

directions: Black highbush blueberry is a wetland-loving native shrub of the eastern United States, ranging south into the Florida panhandle, closely related to and often confused with Vaccinium corymbosum but distinguished by its blackish young twigs and shiny black berries that lack the pale waxy bloom of common highbush blueberry. It naturally colonizes swamp edges, bogs, and pond margins, making it a strong choice for rain gardens and consistently moist, acidic sites where standard highbush blueberry cultivars often struggle. Plants sucker gently to form loose thickets over time and provide the same white urn-shaped spring flowers and valuable wildlife fruit as their more widely cultivated relative, with good red fall color as a bonus.
